title: The Divine Mercy chaplet
hook: on rosary beads: eternal Father, I offer you, and for the sake of his sorrowful passion

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was devotion: a practice freely chosen, that grows around the liturgy and leads back to it. Your line was optional, and loved. Did anyone tell you about theirs? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

A string of beads with a small crucifix at the end. Anyone would call it a rosary, and it is. But the prayer moving through it today is not the rosary. Someone holding those beads on a bus whispers one short line on each small bead, over and over: for the sake of his sorrowful passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world. Same beads, a different prayer. It takes a few minutes. Saint Faustina recorded it in her diary, and it's now prayed far from her convent. Today: how it's built, and what it's asking for.
screen: `THE SAME BEADS.` → `A DIFFERENT PRAYER.` → `HAVE MERCY ON US AND ON THE WHOLE WORLD.`

segments.voice: It's built from two movements that take turns. First, an offering. On each large bead, the person praying speaks to God the Father: eternal Father, I offer you. And what's offered is Christ himself, his body and blood, soul and divinity, for our sins and those of the whole world. That's a bold thing to say at a kitchen table. It echoes the Mass, where the Church offers Christ to the Father. Here, one person with a string of beads joins that offering in a small way. Second, the asking. On each small bead, the same line: for the sake of his sorrowful passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world. The reason given isn't the person's own goodness. It's Christ's suffering. In Luke, Jesus tells of a man who prays in that spirit. A tax collector stands far back in the Temple, won't lift his eyes, strikes his breast, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." No list of achievements. Just the request. Third, the plural. The chaplet never asks mercy for me alone. It's us, and the whole world. Whoever prays it on that bus is asking mercy for the driver, the stranger across the aisle, the people in the news they can't stand. Last, the ending. The chaplet closes by calling God holy, holy and mighty, holy and immortal, and asking once more for mercy. Those titles echo an old hymn of the Eastern churches called the Trisagion, the thrice-holy. So a prayer recorded by a Polish sister ends on words the East has long sung. People pray it alone, in groups, at bedsides, and at three in the afternoon, which is tomorrow's story.
screen: `FIRST, AN OFFERING TO THE FATHER.` · `THEN, THE ASKING.` · `US, AND THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `IT ENDS ON THE THRICE-HOLY.` · then, large: `O GOD, BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray it once, or simply walk through its shape. Take one slow breath first. If you have beads, hold them. If not, your fingers will do. If you pray, you can say the whole chaplet as a prayer card or your parish gives it. If you'd rather keep it simple, take only the short line from the small beads, have mercy on us and on the whole world, and let it pass slowly a few times. Each time, let a different face come to mind: someone close, someone far away, someone hard to love. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
The Divine Mercy chaplet. A short prayer on rosary beads, recorded by Saint Faustina: Christ offered to the Father, and mercy asked for us and for the whole world. Today's word.
Your line: have mercy on us. Today, when someone gets on your nerves, say the line silently, and let the us include them. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Catholics who keep the Divine Mercy devotion pray the chaplet on ordinary rosary beads, alone or in groups, often at three in the afternoon and especially around Divine Mercy Sunday.

fork.reveal: he asks only for mercy, and Jesus says he went home justified. the chaplet's small beads ask in the same spirit.

original.note: Greek: Lord, have mercy. Still sung at Mass; the chaplet's plea belongs to the same family of prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chaplet is a rosary with a different name.
what it means: the same beads carrying a different prayer: Christ offered to the Father, and mercy asked for us and the whole world.
what a scholar hears: the chaplet's closing, holy God, holy mighty one, holy immortal one, echoes the Trisagion, an old hymn of the Eastern liturgies.
